title: Sudden arrhythmic death syndrome (SADS) | NHS inform
text:
Sudden arrhythmic death syndrome (SADS)
Sudden arrhythmic death syndrome (SADS) is when someone dies suddenly and unexpectedly from a
cardiac arrest
but there’s no clear cause.
What causes SADS?
SADS usually happens if there’s a dangerous heart rhythm known as a fatal arrhythmia. Heart rhythm problems can be caused by a fault in the electrical system that makes the heart beat.
Sometimes the condition that causes heart rhythm problems is inherited.
Inherited heart conditions
are a group of conditions that are passed on through families.
Some people with an inherited heart condition don’t have any symptoms. This means some families only find out they’re affected by an inherited heart condition after a sudden death.
How is SADS diagnosed?
If a death is sudden or unexplained it must be reported to the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service (COPFS). They have responsibility for investigating all sudden or unexplained deaths.
Sometimes COPFS may need to arrange a fuller investigation. They may organise a post-mortem examination or ask the police to make enquiries. Sometimes they’ll need to do both.
A post-mortem is when a pathologist examines the body to find out why someone died.
The pathologist will give COPFS a report with their findings. A Victim Information Officer (VIA officer) from COPFS will then contact the person’s relatives. They’ll provide information on the next steps.
A death may be labelled as SADS when the cause of death is still uncertain after a post-mortem has taken place. This is because some inherited heart conditions can’t be seen during a post-mortem as the heart will look normal. These inherited heart conditions are called channelopathies.
The death investigation process
Watch this video from the
COPFS
for more information on the death investigation process.
Genetic testing
A pathologist may recommend genetic testing if they find that the death was caused by a heart condition that may be inherited. They may also recommend it if they can’t find a cause of death.
A small sample of tissue (usually 2cm of spleen) may be stored during the post-mortem for genetic testing.
Family members may be referred to a local inherited heart conditions service. They’ll review if genetic testing is needed and personalise it to your family’s needs.
The Network for Inherited Cardiac Conditions Scotland (NICCS)
has further information on genetic testing and inherited heart conditions.
Sudden cardiac death
Sudden cardiac death (SCD) is an umbrella term for all sudden, unexpected deaths that are due to heart problems.
SADS falls into this category along with other sudden deaths where a heart problem is found during the post-mortem. For example, a blockage in an artery or a change in the structure of the heart.
Unascertained death
Sometimes a death may be recorded as ‘unascertained’ when the cause of death isn’t clear.
The pathologist may still recommend extra tests for inherited heart conditions if the cause of death is ‘unascertained’.
Where to get support
The news of a sudden death is traumatic. It’s hard to come to terms with and you may feel strong emotions like grief, anger and disbelief.
You get support and information from:
Cardiac Risk in the Young (CRY)
– provide help to families after the sudden cardiac death of a young person
The British Heart Foundation
– provide information for anyone who has lost a loved one
Sudden Arrhythmic Death UK
– support anyone affected by cardiac arrest, cardiac conditions or sudden cardiac death
Chest, Heart and Stroke Scotland
– provide support to anyone who has performed CPR or has seen someone receiving CPR
Cruse Scotland
– provide support for bereaved adults, children and families across Scotland
